items.originalTitle: 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?
items.author: VicOne
items.title: 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?
items.summary: This article is brought to you by VicOne . VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others. Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers. Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots. These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster , and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations . What AI changes about vulnerability discovery Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities. When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change. Where the findings sit across the robot lifecycle VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled. Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed. VicOne The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage. Development and training: Hidden changes can reach the finished robot A team downloads a pretrained model to adapt for its robot. Loading a malicious file could give an attacker access to the training system, allowing changes to training data or the model itself. A manipulated model could behave normally during routine testing but respond incorrectly to a particular object, scene, or command after deployment. The risk can enter through a tool the team trusts, before anyone attacks the robot directly. Simulation and validation: A passing test could give false confidence Importing a compromised scene or robot model could give an attacker access to the simulation environment. With sufficient control, the attacker could alter simulated sensor readings, physical conditions, or test results. A robot could then appear to pass tests that should have exposed unsafe behavior, leading the team to approve it for real-world use on the basis of misleading evidence. Deployment and runtime: Operators could lose visibility or control An attacker could exploit weaknesses to change files that influence motion planning or send malicious map data that crashes the operator’s monitoring display. Compromising a remote-operation computer could also put the instructions sent to the robot at risk. Depending on the system and its safeguards, these weaknesses could alter robot movement or leave operators unable to see what is happening and respond promptly. These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior. In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised. Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne A published patch still needs to be proven safe AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior. An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined. Three questions can help teams respond: Where do we use the affected software? Include training computers, simulation environments, and deployed robots. What could the weakness change? Assess whether it could affect models, test results, operator visibility, or robot behavior. How do we verify protection? Confirm that the fix addresses the weakness and that the updated system still operates as intended. When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared. From discovery to safer deployment As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior. That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation. Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation. VicOne Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change. For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper, “ Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On .”

items.title: The Nice Ones review – invasion of the sunny personality snatchers
items.summary: Peter Stylianou’s watchably unsettling tale of unbalanced minds and Unidentified Aerial Phenomena does its best to please Drone shots are two-a-penny in cinema these days, but it’s a mark of this £80,000 British indie sci-fi’s visual astuteness that it largely avoids them in a film plagued by drone-like entities. Instead, it takes a suggestive approach: protagonist Kate (Joelle Rae) is staring out of the window on a car journey, up into the night sky, when a pinprick of light flares out before shooting out a laser towards the ground – then darting off into a cloudbank. Kate chews over this anomaly with boyfriend Dale (Emrhys Cooper), en route to a get-together of his old uni gang in a countryside Airbnb. Already not at ease among his mates, Kate gets a ribbing when she repeats her UFO story (or Unidentified Aerial Phenomena, as they are called these days). And there are knowing glances about her psychiatric history: she once fended off an abusive boyfriend at knifepoint, insisting he was possessed. But if she is delusional, then it seems to be spreading: her one ally, spacey teacher Shelly (Ayvianna Snow), re-enters the room after a suspiciously long fag break, marvelling about how they will all imminently join “the light”.

items.originalTitle: ‘Partly the movie’s fault I’m a writer at all’: why Wonder Boys is my feelgood movie
items.author: Duncan Riddell
items.title: ‘Partly the movie’s fault I’m a writer at all’: why Wonder Boys is my feelgood movie
items.summary: The latest in our series of writers picking their most comforting rewatches is a tribute to Curtis Hanson’s insightful 2000 comedy drama I’m allergic to movies and books about writers. Washed-up novelists, aspiring screenwriters, creative writing professors in the throes of a midlife crisis who cheat on their wives – take your pick. Chalk it up to my being a writer who for two decades wrote continually and fruitlessly about writers. And yet, I love Wonder Boys, Curtis Hanson’s 2000 comedy drama about a rumpled creative writing professor who can’t seem to finish his second novel and is having an affair with his boss’s wife. It’s partly the movie’s fault I’m a writer at all. I saw Wonder Boys on its opening weekend, when I was 17, and the notion of poring over novels with kindred spirits in a sun-dappled seminar room at some leafy liberal arts college – where I’d find myself a year later – held endless appeal. Even the misadventures of the film’s professor, Grady Tripp (Michael Douglas, never better), seemed romantic to me. On the eve of his university’s annual literary festival, Grady’s wife leaves him. His lover, Sara, announces she’s pregnant with his child. And James Leer, his brilliant but troubled student, who can rattle off Hollywood suicides in alphabetical order, shows up at the festival’s kick-off party cradling what may or may not be a cap gun. Grady responds to all this with the urgency of a veteran pot smoker – which he is.

items.originalTitle: Democrats Call for Probe Into Military Leaders as U.S. Army Whistleblower Alleges Warnings Were Dismissed Ahead of Deadly Iran Attack
items.author: Miranda Jeyaretnam
items.title: Democrats Call for Probe Into Military Leaders as U.S. Army Whistleblower Alleges Warnings Were Dismissed Ahead of Deadly Iran Attack
items.summary: U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth salutes as a U.S. Army carry team moves a flag-draped transfer case containing the remains of Sgt. 1st Class Noah L. Tietjens at Dover Air Force Base in Delaware on March 7, 2026. —Roberto Schmidt—Getty Images An American soldier has alleged that U.S. military leaders dismissed concerns ahead of an Iranian attack that killed six servicemembers on March 1. The complaint, submitted Friday to the House and Senate Armed Services committees and first reported by CBS on Sunday, alleges that U.S. Army leaders did not heed warnings about thin fortifications at a command post at Kuwait’s Port Shuaiba. Iran launched a retaliatory drone attack on the command post a day after the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Feb. 28. It remains the deadliest attack on American troops since 2021. Over the eight months of the war, a total of 23 U.S. servicemembers have died . Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom, who filed the complaint and was among the dozens wounded in the attack, called the event a “tactical failure” by “the Army, our leadership, and myself.” Ramsbottom said he had twice raised concerns about the lack of protection from aerial attacks to his superiors but was told, “We don’t have to worry about protection.” He said in an interview with CBS that a counter-drone system “never arrived at Shuaiba and we don’t know if it was ever even ordered to or requested.” He also alleged that the post had “no physician, no fixed aid station, and only one ambulance.” A day after the attack, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the command post suffered casualties despite its fortifications not because of a lack of preparedness. “Every once in a while you might have one, unfortunately, we call it a squirter that makes its way through [air defenses]. And in that particular case it happened to hit a tactical operations center that was fortified,” Hegseth said at a press conference. “But these are powerful weapons.” The Pentagon announced an investigation into the attack on March 3, and the Associated Press reported that it had concluded in June, with a private briefing to families of the slain servicemembers in July. The findings of the investigation have not been publicly disclosed, although widow Michelle Tietjens told CBS that officials acknowledged no mistakes. Ramsbottom’s attorneys separately requested an independent investigation into the attack after filing his Nov. 13 complaint. TIME has reached out to the Pentagon and U.S. Central Command for comment. Disputed accounts Around a week before the U.S. and Israel launched their attacks on Iran, around 70 members of the U.S. Army’s 103rd Sustainment Command were relocated from Camp Arifjan, a major U.S. base south of Kuwait City, to the smaller outpost at Port of Shuaiba. Days after the war began, Hegseth told reporters that the Defense Department prioritized protecting U.S. troops and moving “the vast majority … off the X, out of the range of Iranian fire.” The facility, situated in the civilian port on Kuwait’s southern coast, was within range of Iranian missiles. The Washington Post reported in July that military leaders had ignored intelligence warnings that the post was a probable Iranian target. CBS reported in March that the post was surrounded by T-walls, steel-reinforced concrete barriers that provide protection from mortars and rockets. Ramsbottom told Colorado news station KOAA in April that the facility was protected from “legacy threats” like mortar fire and car bombs, but not from modern aerial attacks, such as by drones or missiles. Other survivors of the attack told CBS in April that the unit “was unprepared to provide any defense for itself. It was not a fortified position.” One soldier described the fort as “a bunch of little tin buildings where we can set up makeshift offices.” The Post reported that a 2021 photograph showed what appeared to be a thin metal rooftop over the building, although it was not clear whether any reinforcement existed underneath. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell rejected reporting that the position was not well-protected. “A Tactical Operations Center is not a ‘makeshift office space.’ The secure facility was fortified with 6-foot walls,” he posted on March 3. “Every possible measure has been taken to safeguard our troops — at every level,” Parnell wrote. Multiple news outlets previously reported that no sirens sounded to alert troops before the deadly strike. CBS reported in March that sirens had occasionally gone off after a drone had already entered the base in previous incidents. CBS reported in April that incoming missile alarms had sounded several hours before the attack, alerting around 60 troops to take cover when a ballistic missile flew overhead, and that an all-clear alert had sounded around 30 minutes before the Iranian drone hit. Troops told the outlet that officers had removed their helmets and resumed work at their desks after the all-clear alert. Soldiers told the Post that the threat warning system was initially not working when a team was sent to scout the post before troops were relocated there. They said repairs had been made to get it operational before the strike happened. U.S. Army Central previously said in statements to media outlets that the alarm system at the facility was working at the time of the attack. Democrats call for probe The whistleblower complaint adds fuel to the fire as Democrats plan to launch congressional investigations into the Trump Administration’s handling of the war when they take control of both chambers of Congress in January. In September, Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Rep. Pat Ryan of New York called for public hearings, citing earlier whistleblower reports about delayed medical care for wounded servicemembers, mistreatment of families, and concerns around the Army’s investigation into the attack. Rep. Maggie Goodlander of New Hampshire described the handling of the attack as “a profound failure of leadership” and said “the Pentagon cannot be allowed to stonewall Congress.” Democrats and some Republicans have also called for Hegseth to step down or face impeachment , and the latest allegations are likely to intensify scrutiny of his leadership. Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D, Conn.), the ranking member on the Senate’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, reportedly sent a letter on Sunday to the Pentagon requesting a classified briefing with Hegseth and “all force protection assessments” for the post. “I’m again demanding full disclosure about the Port Shuaiba attack—an accounting of misjudgments by political appointees likely led to increased vulnerability & greater casualties,” Blumenthal posted on social media on Sunday night. “The families of the six fallen servicemembers, the wounded survivors, & the American people deserve full transparency & accountability,” he added in another post . “It is time for a reckoning.”

items.originalTitle: Delaware hit by rare November tornado
items.author: Megan Davies for MetDesk
items.title: Delaware hit by rare November tornado
items.summary: Meanwhile, severe thunderstorms bring hailstones the size of baseballs in Argentina The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989. Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. A round of severe thunderstorms moved through the central Córdoba province on Friday, bringing hailstones up to the size of a baseball (about 7.5cm in diameter). Parts of the province recorded up to 73mm of rainfall in just six hours early on Saturday. Such storms are common at this time of year. Water vapour from the Amazon meeting the Andes quickly condenses, resulting in massive cloud formations often associated with heavy downpours, lightning, tornadoes and large hailstones.

items.originalTitle: Inside the Denver gathering where Democrats’ upbeat, Obama-era feel meets the 2028 race
items.title: Inside the Denver gathering where Democrats’ upbeat, Obama-era feel meets the 2028 race
items.summary: DENVER — Live music, concert-style campaign posters and a packed schedule of Democratic leaders set the scene in Denver, where party strategists and potential 2028 contenders gathered to celebrate midterm gains and start shaping what comes next. The industrial-style venue, with indoor and outdoor spaces, gave the two-day "What’s Next" gathering a festival feel. Democrats moved between political programming, live music and social events. Beneath the party atmosphere, potential contenders tested their messages and sized up the field, as Democrats began jockeying over the party’s direction and who might lead it in 2028. The event had an unmistakably Obama-era feel, with its hopeful message and celebratory campaign atmosphere. DEMS DESCEND ON DENVER TO SIZE UP 2028; WE ASKED WHO WANTS IN THE RACE Matt Corridon, a Democratic strategist and communications adviser at Majority Democrats, said the comparison made sense. "The theme of that campaign was hope, and a lot of folks who are here now either worked on that campaign or were inspired by that campaign," Corridon said. "I think one of the themes of this event is hopefulness for the Democratic Party moving forward. It’s a comparison that doesn’t shock me." That hopeful energy showed up in the event’s posters and playful swag, some of which Ahmad Ali, communications director for the Searchlight Institute, helped design. DEMOCRATS RIDE MIDTERM WAVE AS 2028 HOPEFULS GATHER IN DENVER TO MAP THEIR NEXT MOVES "I think we’re seeing a Democratic Party that is younger, brighter and way more emboldened to achieve what it wants to," Ali told Fox News Digital. "So this conference, its aesthetics, whether it’s the posters you see, the fun hats, all that — it just speaks to the confidence of the era." Ali said the party’s energy could signal a break from what he described as a period of political stagnation, with voters looking for new choices in 2028 . He pointed to former President Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign and President Donald Trump’s 2024 victory as moments that captured the political mood, while arguing that the Biden era did not carry the same cultural force. "We are at the end of the Trump era, but we’re also at the end of whatever the sort of period of stuckness has plagued the Democratic Party," Ali said. "And I think that is very important, not just for Democrats, but also for all voters, because now maybe they’re going to have better options come 2028." The gathering offered a first glimpse of how Democrats hope to turn their midterm momentum into a path to 2028.

items.originalTitle: Democrats could raise the minimum wage next year. How high should they go?
items.author: Rachel Cohen
items.title: Democrats could raise the minimum wage next year. How high should they go?
items.summary: A decade after the Democratic Party rallied around the Fight for 15 movement, how high to raise the minimum wage — and how fast — is becoming a defining economic question for the new majority. | Erik McGregor/LightRocket via Getty Images In the wake of the midterm elections in which Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate , a growing number of politicians and activists have begun calling, publicly and privately, for Congress to seize the moment and pass the first federal minimum wage increase in 17 years. After running campaigns centered on the cost of living, Democrats and their allies say raising the $7.25 federal minimum closer to a “living wage” — i.e., enough for a full-time worker to cover basics like rent, food, and healthcare — is the obvious next step for their affordability mandate. A minimum wage increase also has a political advantage because businesses, not the government, cover the cost, meaning it has little effect on the deficit and doesn’t compete with other priorities for federal dollars. “I’ve been talking with a lot of different Democrats on the Hill and they’ve been calling it a first 100-day issue,” said Jared Bernstein, who chaired President Joe Biden’s Council of Economic Advisers and is now at the liberal Center for American Progress. Rahm Emanuel, who is widely expected to run for president in 2028, has been urging Democrats to act , and it was a top issue for the party when he ran its campaign arm in 2006. “Pass a minimum wage $20 by 2030,” he said on Vox’s Today, Explained podcast after the election. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) has also been making media rounds calling for raising the wage to “at least $20 bucks an hour.” On Thursday, Hakeem Jeffries, who’s expected to be the House speaker, identified raising the wage as a priority, but ducked press questions about specifics. Key takeaways Many Democrats want to raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to about $20 an hour by 2030. Sen. Chris Murphy’s bill would go to $25. Most research finds past increases raised pay without costing many jobs. But few places have set a minimum that high relative to local wages, so economists don’t know where the limit is. Critics warn a high national minimum could hurt lower-wage states the most and lead employers to raise prices or cut hours, benefits, and training. Raising the minimum wage is popular across party lines, and because the cost falls on businesses and their customers rather than taxpayers, it adds little to the federal deficit. A decade after the party rallied around the “Fight for 15” movement, how high to raise the minimum wage — and how fast — is becoming a defining economic question for the new Democratic majority, as well as in states where they have new governing trifectas. In Pennsylvania, Gov. Josh Shapiro has pledged to sign a $15 minimum wage bill , while in Wisconsin, Gov.-elect David Crowley has targeted a gradual increase to $20 . In recent years, a wave of research built on the 30 states that raised their own minimums has convinced many economists that modest increases cost few, if any, jobs. That evidence, plus voters’ anger about the cost of living, has rallied progressive experts around a new federal benchmark equal to two-thirds of the hourly median wage, or roughly $20 by 2030. But that threshold is also near the upper end of what researchers have actually studied, and even economists who support it acknowledge that no one knows how high the minimum wage can go before it starts costing a significant number of jobs or increasing prices at a time when inflation is a major concern. Skeptics warn that a national minimum that high could hit the country’s lowest-wage places hardest, just as AI introduces new threats to the jobs young and less-experienced workers depend on. Still, raising the minimum wage is popular with voters, and even some Republicans have expressed openness to cutting a deal. “You want to raise the minimum wage? I’m for that,” Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO) told reporters last week . The last wage increase was signed by a Republican president after Democrats won both chambers of Congress in the 2006 midterms, much as they did this month. Trump, who has previously called the $7.25 minimum wage “ a very low number ” recently told Politico he doesn’t want to “just be sitting there for two years vetoing everything.” Some Democrats want to go even further, like Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut, whose bill introduced over the summer would require big companies to pay $25 within about five years and smaller ones by the late 2030s. Murphy makes the case for his bill less on labor-market research and more on economic fairness. “It’s not like we can’t pay a $25 minimum wage,” Murphy said after announcing his legislation. “We just choose not to.” And in New York City, Mayor Zohran Mamdani ran on a $30 minimum wage by 2030 , though the plan hasn’t gotten traction in the state legislature, which would have to approve it. As Democrats look to act in 2027 and beyond, the empirical debate over how high the minimum wage can safely go is getting entangled with the populist one over how high the party should aim. These debates are especially important because the party may have far more power to raise wages than they expected before their midterm wins, both in Congress and in states and cities around the country. While previous efforts in Congress have been stymied by procedural barriers, Senate Democrats are now within reach of a filibuster-proof majority as soon as 2029. Far from a messaging exercise, the question of how high wages should be at the bottom is now a live policy issue that the party needs to take seriously — with potentially severe consequences if they misstep. How Democrats work through these tensions will shape both how much low-wage workers might gain, and what they might lose, and how much of the party’s answer to the cost of living rests on the minimum wage at all. From $15 to $20 (and beyond) Beginning in 2012 and backed by the Service Employees International Union, fast-food workers walked off their jobs, demanding $15 an hour and the right to form a union. The Fight for 15 became a national movement, spreading to other sectors like academia, airports, and childcare, and it pushed past the position of President Barack Obama and congressional Democrats, who were calling then for a $10.10 minimum . In 2015, congressional Democrats introduced the Raise the Wage Act, which would have increased the federal minimum wage to $12 an hour by 2020 . Hillary Clinton campaigned on a $12 minimum in the 2016 primary, while Sanders leaned into the $15 standard. By the time the general election rolled around, even with Clinton as the nominee, the Democratic Party platform had embraced $15, and by 2017, Democrats, now with Sanders as the Senate’s lead sponsor, updated the Raise the Wage Act to a $15 target. The House passed the $15 bill in 2019, but it died in the Republican-controlled Senate. In 2021, the Senate parliamentarian blocked Democrats from adding it to Biden’s pandemic relief package, though it’s possible a future Congress might feature a different parliamentarian with a different perspective. In July 2023, Sanders and Rep. Bobby Scott raised the bill’s target again, this time to $17 an hour . But while progress in Washington stalled, leaders around the country took action. Since 2014, 28 states and Washington, DC, have passed laws raising their minimum wages, and nearly 70 cities and counties now have minimums higher than their state’s. Some of the increases came through legislation, while others came from ballot measure campaigns, including in red states like Arkansas, Florida, Missouri, and Nebraska. Eighteen states and DC now have minimums of $15 or more. Though raising the minimum wage has long drawn support across party lines, in June, Oklahoma voters decisively rejected a measure that would have raised the state’s minimum from $7.25 to $15 by 2029. Opponents argued that the raise , plus automatic yearly increases tied to inflation, would have driven up prices and hurt small businesses. (The vote also came during a low-turnout June primary , when only about a quarter of registered voters cast ballots.) That same month, Murphy introduced the Living Wage for All Act , outflanking Sanders’s Raise the Wage Act from the left. Murphy, who is also widely expected to run for president, has argued that Democrats should lean harder into economic populism to win back the working class. A $25 minimum wage is “the bare minimum of what workers deserve — and of what workers should expect from their leaders,” he declared in an essay accompanying his bill’s release. “It’s also what’s best for the health of our economy and country.” Murphy and Sanders discussed the Living Wage for All Act earlier this year, a Murphy spokesperson told me, adding that “conversations among the caucus are ongoing as to how best raise the minimum wage across the nation.” What the research says A generation ago, efforts to boost the minimum wage ran into a recurring problem: a widespread consensus among economists that increases came with serious trade-offs, like fewer jobs and higher prices. And not just free-market conservatives, but more liberal economists like former New York Times columnist Paul Krugman, who in 1998 chastised activists who believed wages “can be set based on considerations of justice, not supply and demand, without unpleasant side effects.” But that consensus quietly shifted over the years as more states and cities experimented with ambitious wage increases — and ran into fewer difficulties than expected. Proponents of a federal minimum wage of $20 or more often point to the work of Arin Dube, an economist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and one of the most widely cited researchers on the topic. In a 2024 meta-analysis co-authored with Ben Zipperer from the left-leaning Economic Policy Institute, Dube reviewed nearly 90 studies and found that most showed minimum-wage increases raised workers’ total pay with little job loss. Critics still point to places like Seattle and California as warnings, where studies have found that Seattle’s minimum-wage increase cut hours for low-wage workers and California’s $20 fast-food wage cost jobs, though other researchers dispute those findings. But in general, there were few glaring cautionary tales in a sea of state and local increases. Dube says years of minimum-wage research, including comparisons of the 30 states that raised their minimums with the 20 that didn’t, have changed how economists understand the labor market. Economics 101 would suggest that raising labor costs means employers hire fewer workers. But many employers have enough power in their local job market to pay less than workers would earn elsewhere, so a higher minimum can raise pay without making those jobs unprofitable. “The idea is employers have some choice when it comes to setting pay,” Dube told me. Paying workers more can also make it easier to hire and retain staff, and workers tend to be more productive when they’re paid more, he added. Dube said this helps explain why pay has grown faster in the 30 states that raised their minimums than in the 20 that didn’t, while job growth has been “virtually identical” across both groups, including in low-wage industries like restaurants and retail. Some of the higher cost does get passed on to customers, Dube acknowledged, but not by much. “Maybe middle-class and higher-income families pay a little bit more for the burger,” he said. In light of the research, progressive economists have begun rallying around a new federal target, to raise the federal minimum to two-thirds of the median hourly wage, or roughly $17 today and about $20 by 2030. That would be “a fairly reasonable but strong minimum wage policy,” Dube told me, meaning a big enough increase to help millions of workers, but not so high that it would go “far outside of our evidence base.” I asked Dube about Murphy’s bill, which mostly tracks the path he describes but would require big companies, those with at least 500 workers or $1 billion in revenue, to pay $25 an hour within five years. He said that could push their minimum above the two-thirds benchmark for a while, a “temporary overshooting” before it eventually lines back up with two-thirds of the median. Murphy’s $25 figure is drawn from MIT’s living wage calculations , and his office also points to what the minimum would be worth if it had kept pace with inflation and productivity since 1968. “A minimum wage in the United States of America should be a living wage,” Murphy said when he introduced the bill. In an interview, Patrick Oakford, the director of the Worker Power and Economic Security program at the Roosevelt Institute, a progressive think tank, told me supporters of a $20 wage were not working backward from a clear number, but instead chose the target based on the available evidence. “Any rational person who looks fairly at this body of research can really only come to one conclusion, which is that raising the minimum wage does not lead to significant job loss,” he told me, even at two-thirds of the median. Earlier this year, though, in a report Oakford authored , he also grounded the two-thirds target in what the minimum wage should accomplish: At that level, he wrote, a full-time minimum wage would get much closer to what it actually costs a single adult to live, and it would match the target the United Kingdom set and reached in 2024. As for critics who note that most US studies looked at minimums well below two-thirds of the median, Oakford argues that the studies that went higher, including of California’s $20 fast-food wage, haven’t found a cliff, a point where job losses suddenly spike. “My read of the research is that two-thirds of the median is a legitimate upper bound, but more cautious approaches are also defensible,” Bernstein, of the Center for American Progress, told me. How high is too high? Other economists I spoke with were less supportive. “Two-thirds of the median makes me pretty nervous, and numbers like $20 and $25 an hour are entirely ungrounded,” said Jason Furman, who chaired the Council of Economic Advisers in the Obama administration. Furman agrees that small increases in the minimum wage haven’t cost many jobs, but in his view there’s little good evidence on bigger increases, and the federal floor should be built for the lowest-wage states, like Mississippi, since higher-wage states can always go further on their own. In lower-wage states, the concern is that the same $20 minimum would be a much bigger shock to employers, who would have to raise pay for a far larger share of their workers, and that’s where economists worry job losses are most likely to show up. Employers also may cut back on worker benefits — a major concern at the moment as health premiums soar — and job training. With AI threatening entry-level jobs, past evidence about whether employers turn to automation to replace low-wage workers may be a poor guide to what comes next. Every economist I spoke with said there’s a point at which a federal minimum wage could be increased too much. “To me all of this doesn’t say don’t do it, but to be careful and moderate,” Furman said. Michael Strain, the director of Economic Policy Studies at the American Enterprise Institute, a conservative think tank, told me he thinks the employment effects of the minimum wage are “genuinely contested,” and he’s “skeptical of excessive certainty,” both from those who insist higher minimums cost no jobs and from those who warn of a surge in unemployment. Strain favors expanding the Earned Income Tax Credit — which costs the government money, but doesn’t affect employers — to help workers with the least experience and fewest options, and argues that the minimum wage is “counterproductive” for those individuals, since it can price them out of jobs. Ryan Bourne, an economist at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank, would prefer no federal minimum wage at all, but says that if there has to be one, it’s best set locally, where policymakers have a clearer sense of their own labor markets. He argues that even if some employers do have the power to hold down wages, that power varies by industry and region, so it doesn’t justify one national number. “If you’re talking about Eagle Pass, Texas; or Hot Springs, Arkansas; or Gadsden, Alabama, this is going to be a really, really big deal,” he said of a $20 or $25 federal standard. There are examples abroad, too. In 2018 and 2019, South Korea raised its minimum wage nearly 30 percent, taking it from 53 percent to 63 percent of the median wage, close to the two-thirds benchmark. A Kansas City Fed study estimated the increases cut employment at manufacturing firms by about 3 percent. But the United Kingdom, by contrast, moved more gradually to around two-thirds of the median , and research has found no robust evidence that it hurt jobs, suggesting the pace of an increase may matter. Every economist I spoke with said there’s a point at which a federal minimum wage could be increased too much. “There would definitely be a point where if the minimum wage is high enough, you would start to see more substantial changes on employment,” Dube told me. When I asked Dube what that too-high point is, he said no one knows, because no state has raised its minimum high enough to find it. One option is to build guardrails into the legislation, like New York did. Under a 2023 law, New York’s minimum wage law has been indexed to rise with inflation, beginning in 2027, unless the economy shows signs of trouble. Earlier this fall, a small decline in jobs triggered that “off-ramp” for the first time, freezing the state’s minimum at $17 downstate and $16 upstate for 2027. (Gov. Kathy Hochul now calls the trigger too sensitive, and has proposed loosening it .) Bernstein of the Center for American Progress summed up the dilemma. “It’s hard to know where the line is,” he said, “until you cross it.”

items.originalTitle: My search for Bologna’s perfect tagliatelle al ragù - the real ‘spag bol’
items.author: Ben Aitken
items.title: My search for Bologna’s perfect tagliatelle al ragù - the real ‘spag bol’
items.summary: The signature dish of Italy’s gastronomic capital is taken far more seriously than its British derivative. So which restaurant does the best ‘tag rag’? I used to eat spag bol three times a week. I’d have it every Friday at my nan’s, every Saturday at my dad’s, and every Tuesday at my mum’s. My nan would lean heavily on Dolmio and add a cheeky splash of Tabasco. My mum would rustle up hers in the time it took the pasta to cook, which gave it a crunchiness that sometimes made me cry (I swear to God, those onions were practically raw). And my dad would let his bubble away for the duration of Gladiators, meaning that by the time it was dished up at the start of Blind Date, it had an intensity that felt positively foreign. I’m not alone in being a big fan of spag bol – the dish is often voted the nation’s favourite, and there’s now even a National Spaghetti Bolognese Day (22 May) – but I do sometimes wonder what it is about this relatively simple import, essentially a combo of mince and tomatoes plonked upon pasta, that has won over millions and withstood the vagaries of time. So I travelled to the dish’s motherland, Bologna, to unlock its secrets and hunt down some prime examples.
